Sha'arei Kedusha, Introduction 1: Thus says the young Chaim, son of the honored Rabbi Yosef Vital, of blessed memory:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Introduction 2: I have seen those who aspire to ascend to the heights — and they are few — yearning to rise, yet the ladder is hidden from their eyes; they search the ancient books to seek and find paths of life, the way they should walk and the deeds they should do, to raise their souls to their supernal root and to cleave to Him, blessed be He — for that is the eternal perfection, as it was with the prophets, who clove to their Maker all their days, and through that cleaving the Holy Spirit rested upon them, to teach them along which way light dwells, to illuminate their eyes with the mysteries of the Torah, as King David, peace be upon him, prayed, "Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of Your Torah," and to guide them on a straight path, to walk toward the dwelling-place appointed for them together with those who ascend to the heights. After them came the early pious ones (chasidim), called "Perushim" (the separated ones), who sought to follow in the footsteps and the circuits of the prophets and to become like them — in caves of rock and in the deserts — and they separated themselves from the ways of ordinary people; some of them lived apart even within their own houses, after the manner of those who dwell in the wilderness, and all day and all night they never fell silent, praising their Creator through engaging in Torah and through the songs of King David, peace be upon him, which gladden the heart, until their thought clove, with tremendous force and longing, to the supernal lights. They persisted in this all their days, until they rose to the level of the Holy Spirit, and they prophesied without ceasing — as Onkelos translated, "and they did not cease." And although "no two are alike," the exact manner of their ways and their practices has not been preserved for us — how these holy men served the blessed Name — so let us do likewise.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Introduction 3: And so the hearts, and likewise the knowledge, of the generations who came after them grew smaller, and those possessed of the Holy Spirit ceased to be; they journeyed on to their rest, leaving us to sighs, thirsty and hungry, until despair took root in the hearts of men regarding the pursuit of this wondrous wisdom. And if two or three berries are found at the top of the bough — one from a city and two from a clan — seeking water, there is none, for all vision has been sealed up, for the reason that no book has recorded the manner of its practice, of drawing near to approach the Holy of Holies within.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Introduction 4: There were some among them who would adjure the angels by the power of the holy Names, hoping for light, and behold — darkness; for these were angels of a very low order, appointed over the workings of this world, and they themselves are a mixture of good and evil, and they themselves cannot attain the truth and the supernal lights, and so they reveal to those who invoke them a mixture of matters — good and evil, truth and falsehood — and idle things concerning cures, and the science of alchemy, and the workings of amulets and adjurations; and these too "have erred through wine and gone astray through strong drink." Would that their hearts had been set instead on occupying themselves with Torah and mitzvot, and let them draw the a fortiori inference from those four great men of Israel who entered the Pardes, of whom not one escaped unharmed, save that elder saint, Rabbi Akiva — and even he, the ministering angels sought to thrust him away, had the Lord not helped him — he entered in peace and departed in peace.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Introduction 5: And the truth is that they sought great levels, close to prophecy, and therefore some of them were put in danger. But as for us — would that we merit even a little of the Holy Spirit, such as the revelation of Elijah, of blessed memory, which many have merited, as is well known, and such as the revelation of the souls of the righteous, mentioned many times in the Sefer HaTikkunim. Moreover, even in our own time I have seen holy men merit all of this. And there are some whose own soul, when purified exceedingly, is revealed to the person and guides him in all his ways. All these are attainable paths, even in our time, for those who are worthy of them. But truly, great discernment and many trials are needed to ascertain the truth, lest some other, impure spirit was with him. All this will be explained in Part Three, Gate Eight.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Introduction 6: Therefore the spirit within me pressed me to give release to the Perushim, and to strengthen their right hand, to teach them the way they should walk. And so I composed this work, small in quantity but great in quality — "the wise shall shine" — and I called it Sha'arei Kedushah (Gates of Holiness). In it I will explain secrets that the earlier ones before us did not fathom, for I received them by word of mouth from a holy man, an angel of the Lord of Hosts, my teacher the Ari, Rabbi Yitzchak Luria, of blessed memory. And since these are mysteries of the world and hidden secrets, I will reveal a handbreadth and conceal a thousand cubits, and I will open, with difficulty, the gates of holiness like the eye of a needle, and whoever is worthy will merit to enter into the innermost chamber. And may the good Lord not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Introduction 7: And I have divided it into four parts:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Introduction 8: The first part concerns the conduct of the way of piety (chasidut) and asceticism (perishut), which brings one to the Holy Spirit, and it too is divided into six gates. The second part concerns rebukes, and an explanation of the punishment and reward for positive and negative commandments, and is divided into eight gates. And the third part concerns the conduct for attaining the Holy Spirit itself, and is divided into eight gates. And the fourth part concerns the modes of the unifications (yichudim) themselves, through which the Holy Spirit is attained, as I have examined and tested, and which have been verified through me.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Introduction 9: And I will write out their details by way of an enumerated list of signs. And so I begin, with the help of God.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Introduction 10: The first part is divided into six gates. The first, to make known the great extent of the flaw caused by a person's sin regarding the commandments. The second, on the flaw caused by unseemly character traits. The third, an explanation of the term tzaddik (righteous) or chasid (pious). The fourth, an explanation of the level of the tzaddik in detail. The fifth, an explanation of the level of the chasid in detail. The sixth, an explanation of the conduct of the pious in a very brief manner, encompassing all the gates in this part.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Introduction 11: The second part is divided into eight gates. The first, on rebukes. The second, on the ethical teachings of our Sages, of blessed memory. The third, on the reward of those who fulfill the Torah and its commandments. The fourth, on the punishment for bad character traits. The fifth, on the punishment for forbidden character traits. The sixth, on the punishment for transgressing negative commandments. The seventh, on the reward for positive commandments. The eighth, repentance.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Introduction 12: The third part concerns the conduct for attaining the Holy Spirit, and is divided into eight gates. The first, on the nature of the worlds. The second, on the nature of man. The third, on the obstacles to prophecy. The fourth, on the conditions for prophecy. The fifth, on the quality of prophecy and its particulars. The sixth, on the levels of prophecy. The seventh, on the level of the Holy Spirit attainable in our own time. The eighth, a brief conduct [summary].
Sha'arei Kedusha, Introduction 13: The fourth part: see at the end of the book.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 1:1-3: The First Gate: an explanation of the flaw caused by a person's sins regarding the commandments:

I shall enlighten you and show you how great is the evil of a person who commits any one of the 365 negative commandments of the Lord, which are not to be done, or who refrains from fulfilling any one of the 248 positive commandments which he was commanded to perform:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 1:4: It is known to men of understanding that the body of man is not man himself in respect of the body, for that is called merely the flesh of man, as it is written (Job 10:11), "You have clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews," and further it is written (Exodus 30:32), "upon the flesh of man it shall not be poured," and so on. It follows that man himself is the inwardness, while the body is a kind of single garment in which the intellective soul — which is man himself, while he is in this world — clothes itself; and after his passing, this garment is stripped from him and he is clothed in a pure and clean, spiritual garment, as it is written (Zechariah 3:4), "Remove the filthy garments from him... and I will clothe you with fine apparel" — this is what is called the "garment of the Sages" (challuka de-rabbanan).
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 1:5: And just as a craftsman makes a garment for a person's body in the shape of the body's own limbs, so too, blessed be He, He made the body — which is the garment of the soul — in the very form of the soul's own image, with 248 limbs, and 365 sinews connecting those limbs, in order to draw through them the blood and the life-force from limb to limb like conduits. And after forming the body, He breathed into it a living soul composed of 248 spiritual limbs and 365 spiritual sinews, and these clothed themselves within the body's 248 limbs and 365 sinews; and then the soul's limbs perform their actions by means of the instruments, which are the limbs of the body — like an axe in the hand of the one who hews with it. And the proof of this is that the limbs of the body do not perform their function except while the soul is within them — the eye sees, the ear hears, and so on — and when the soul departs, the windows [of the eyes] darken and all the senses cease to function throughout the 248 limbs.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 1:6: And in the same way, the 365 spiritual sinews of the soul clothe themselves within the 365 sinews of the body, drawing the bodily nourishment, which is the blood, to the 248 limbs of the body, together with the inner spiritual nourishment within it, to sustain the 248 limbs of the soul. And after death no vitality is any longer supplied, and the sinews of the body likewise disintegrate and decay, just as the 248 limbs do, and they become as though they never were. It follows that man himself is nothing other than the intellective soul, which clothes itself in the body — called its garment — in this world.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 1:7: And know that after Adam the first man sinned and ate from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil, both his soul and his body likewise became compounded, each of them, of good and evil — and this is the matter of the venom (zuhama) which the serpent injected into Eve and Adam; and through the evil and the venom that it injected into them, they brought upon themselves illnesses, afflictions, and death for both their soul and their body. This is what is written (Genesis 2:17), "for on the day you eat of it you shall surely die" — the death of the soul and the death of the body.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 1:8: Let us explain the matter of the good and evil that became mixed within them — and see what we shall write further on in Part Three, Gates Two and Three, and you will understand what we write here in this gate. When he sinned with the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil, he caused this admixture throughout all the worlds, and there is nothing that is not composed of good and evil.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 1:9: It follows that the body of man, formed from the four lower elements, is likewise composed of good and evil: the body of man was formed from the good in the four elements — fire, air, water, earth — while from the evil within them there were formed in the body four humors, namely the white one, the black one, the red one, and the green one. And when any one of them, in respect of its evil aspect, overpowers its good aspect, illnesses and afflictions come upon the person, and if it overpowers still further, it can bring death to the person's body.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 1:10: It has already been explained that there was a mixture of good and evil throughout all the worlds, and it follows that this was also so in the soul of man; for it was hewn from four spiritual elements from which all the supernal beings were formed, namely the four letters of the Name Havayah (the Tetragrammaton), blessed be He — and of this it is said (Ezekiel 37:9), "Come from the four winds, O breath..." — and this is called the soul of man itself, on its good side. But God likewise made the counterpart to this, which is called the "wicked man" (adam beliya'al), comprising the four principal categories of damage and the four appearances of leprous plagues, [derived] from the four evil elements; and from there a wicked soul, called the yetzer hara (evil inclination), is drawn to a person. And when this soul overpowers the good soul, damages, afflictions, and illnesses of the soul come upon it, and if it overpowers it still further, it will bring about its death.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 1:11: Now, the pure soul, which is the "fruit," is composed of 613 limbs and sinews, and it clothes itself within the 613 limbs and sinews of the impure soul, called the "peel of the fruit" (kelipat ha-pri); and the two of them together clothe themselves within the 613 limbs and sinews of the body. Thus the limbs of the pure soul are found within the limbs of the wicked soul, and the limbs of the wicked soul are found within the limbs of the body. Now each of these two souls requires spiritual nourishment in order to subsist; and the spiritual nourishment of the holy soul is drawn to it through the fulfillment of the Torah, which is composed of 613 commandments corresponding to the soul's own 613 limbs, and is called "bread," as it is written (Proverbs 9:5), "Come, eat of my bread." And each of the 248 limbs is nourished from the particular commandment corresponding to that limb; and when a person fails to fulfill some commandment, the particular limb corresponding to that commandment likewise loses the nourishment drawn to it from the four letters of the Name Havayah, as it is written (Nehemiah 9:6), "and You give life to them all." And all the commandments depend upon these letters, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said (in the introduction to the Tikkunim): "Yud-Heh corresponds to My Name of 365 [negative commandments], Vav-Heh to My remembrance of 248 [positive commandments]."
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 1:12: And likewise, the four root-elements of his holy soul mentioned above are drawn from these; and it follows that that limb dies entirely. And when holiness departs from it, then the spirit of impurity, from the four elements of his impure soul, clothes itself in it — in the mystery of what our Sages, of blessed memory, said: "Tyre was only filled up from the destruction of Jerusalem" — and so that limb is nourished from defiled bread, polluted from there.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 1:13: This is the meaning of the statement that the wicked, even in their lifetime, are called dead (Berachot 18b) — because the holy soul, which is from the living God, has departed from them, and death, called the "father of the fathers of impurity," rests upon them instead. Likewise, when a person fulfills the 365 negative commandments by refraining from transgressing them — as our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Kiddushin 39b), "if a person sits and does not commit a transgression, he is given reward as one who performs a mitzvah" — there is power in the spiritual nourishment mentioned above, drawn through the fulfillment of the positive commandments, to flow through the conduits, which are the 365 sinews of the soul, to give life to its 248 limbs. And when he transgresses one of those negative commandments, then that particular conduit corresponding to that transgression becomes blocked by the venom of the kelipah's nourishment that clings there; and when the conduit dries up, that limb likewise withers, although it is not removed entirely — just as one who lacks the fulfillment of some positive commandment thereby develops a blemish in it.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 1:14: Therefore a person must search with all his strength to fulfill all 613 commandments; and when he fulfills some positive commandment, he should intend thereby to remove, from the particular limb of his soul corresponding to that commandment, the venom of that kelipah, and then, after the venom departs, the holy limb of that commandment will settle upon him — in the mystery of (Ezekiel 32:27), "and their iniquities shall be upon their bones," for as one rises the other falls. Likewise, when some transgression comes his way, he should refrain from doing it, intending thereby to remove the venom that is in the particular sinew of the soul corresponding to that transgression, so that the spiritual flow drawn through the spiritual conduit can then continue; and through this his soul becomes a throne and a chariot for His holiness, blessed be He — and this is the mystery of "the Patriarchs, they themselves are the Chariot" (Bereishit Rabbah 47:6; Zohar I, 173a).
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 2:1-3:
The Second Gate:
On the flaw caused by unseemly character traits:
Now, the matter of the character traits is that they are implanted in man in the lower soul called the "foundational" (yesodit) soul, which is composed of four aspects — the mineral (domem), the vegetative (tzomeach), the animal (behemit), and the speaking (medaber) — for these too are compounded of good and evil. And upon this soul the good and bad character traits depend, and it is a throne, foundation, and root for the higher, intellective soul, upon which the 613 commandments of the Torah depend, as mentioned above in the First Gate. Therefore the character traits are not counted among the 613 commandments, but they are the essential preconditions for the 613 commandments — for their fulfillment or their nullification — since the intellective soul has no power to fulfill the commandments through the body's 613 limbs except by means of the foundational soul, which is joined to the body itself, in the mystery of (Leviticus 17:14), "for the life of all flesh, its blood is in its soul." Therefore the matter of bad character traits is far, far more grave than the transgressions themselves.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 2:4: By this you will understand what our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 105b): whoever becomes angry, it is as though he worships idols outright — which is the transgression weighed as equal to all 613 commandments. And likewise they said (Sotah) that whoever possesses haughtiness of spirit is as one who denies the fundamental principle of faith, and deserves to be hewn down like an Asherah tree, so that even his dust shall not be stirred — and many statements like these. Understand this well: because these traits are principles and foundations, they were not counted among the 613 commandments that depend on the intellective soul; and it follows that one must be even more careful of bad character traits than of the fulfillment of the positive and negative commandments, for one who possesses good character traits will fulfill all the commandments with ease.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 2:5: By this you will also understand astonishing statements our Sages, of blessed memory, made concerning the character traits: that humility and lowliness bring one to the Holy Spirit, and the Shechinah rests upon him; and Elijah, of blessed memory, said (Kallah Rabbati ch. 5), "The Torah is expounded only to one who is not quick-tempered; I too reveal Myself only to one who is not quick-tempered." And likewise our Sages, of blessed memory, said, in a message sent from there (Sanhedrin 88b): "Who has a share in the World to Come? Whoever is humble and lowly of spirit" — and many statements like these, which mention not the fulfillment of the commandments but only the good character traits. Set these words before your eyes, and you will surely succeed in your ways.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 2:6: Now, just as the four bodily elements are the roots from which the body's 613 limbs were formed, so too the souls of these four elements are the foundations for all good and bad character traits, by means of which the Torah and its commandments — the 613 commandments from the four letters of the Name Havayah mentioned above — are either fulfilled or nullified. And those who fulfill them are the intellective soul, composed of the four spiritual elements from which the 613 limbs of that soul were hewn. Understand this well: how the foundation for fulfilling the commandments is through the good character traits, and likewise the opposite.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 2:7: This is their meaning: it has already been explained that everything God made is composed of good and evil, one corresponding to the other. Now, just as in the four bodily elements — called the material of the elements — good and evil are compounded, and from there come the forces of the body's health or its ailments, which are the four humors — white bile, green bile, black bile, and red bile — so too in the souls, called "forms," the four elements are likewise good and evil in this manner; and from them comes the health of the foundational soul in man, which are the good character traits, or its ailments, which are the bad character traits, drawn from the four impure kelipot within that soul. And when he removes them from himself, the four letters of Havayah, which are the light that gives life to the foundational soul, will clothe themselves within it, and it, together with its body, will become a chariot for His holiness, blessed be He, in the World of Assiyah (Action) — just as was explained regarding the intellective soul itself, through its fulfillment of the commandments.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 2:8: Remember and do not forget that also through engaging in Torah study by way of the four modes of interpretation whose acronym is PaRDeS — peshat (plain meaning), remez (allusion), derash (homiletic exposition), and sod (secret meaning) — one's intellective spirit becomes a throne for the Name Havayah in the World of Yetzirah (Formation); and likewise, through thought and intention, one's intellective soul becomes a throne for the Name Havayah in the World of Beriah (Creation).
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 2:9: Let us return to explaining the four elements which pertain to the acquisition of character traits. Know that all bad character traits are rooted in the four levels of the foundational soul, on the side of the evil and the kelipah within it; therefore all bad character traits are divided into four categories, and these are their details:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 2:10: From the element of fire is drawn pride, called haughtiness of spirit, since it is the lightest and highest of all the elements. Anger is included within it, for it is because of pride that a person becomes angry when things are not done as he wishes; whereas if he were humble of spirit and recognized his own deficiency, he would not become angry at all. It follows that pride and anger are one and the same trait. It has three offshoots: touchiness in one's heart — for were it not for pride, one would not take offense in his heart, just as we explained regarding anger; the seeking of authority and honor, to exalt oneself over other people; and hatred of another for being greater than oneself — this too is a branch of pride.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 2:11: From the element of air is drawn speech, called idle talk — words that serve no purpose at all, whether for the soul or for the body. It has four offshoots: speaking flattery, falsehoods, evil speech (lashon hara), and revealing one's own praises to other people in order to make oneself great in their eyes.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 2:12: From the element of water is drawn the desire for pleasures, for water is what causes every kind of pleasure to grow. It has two offshoots: covetousness — to seize one's fellow's money, wife, and all that is his, in order to take pleasure in them; and envy — envying one's fellow who has great wealth and the like, in order to take pleasure in it.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 2:13: From the element of earth is drawn the trait of sadness in all its particulars, and it has one offshoot: laziness in fulfilling the Torah and the commandments, on account of one's sadness over acquiring the vanities of this world, or over the suffering that comes upon him — so that he is not glad with his lot in anything, and his eye is never satisfied with wealth.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 2:14: It follows that the fathers of all bad character traits are four: pride, together with the anger that is included in and clings to it; idle talk; the desire for pleasures; and sadness — and all four are drawn from the four kelipot of the evil inclination that are in the foundational soul. Their opposites are four good character traits drawn from the four elements of good in the foundational soul. They are: humility, which is the ultimate of lowliness and distances one from every kind of anger that comes through pride; silence — being like a mute, opening one's mouth only for occupying oneself with Torah and mitzvot, or out of necessity for the body's sustenance or for the sake of showing respect to people; disdain for all the pleasures of the body and its unnecessary indulgences; and constant joy in one's lot, for whatever Heaven does is for the good — and also to bestir oneself with the utmost joy in the service of one's Maker, as it is written (Psalms 119:162), "I rejoice at Your word, like one who finds great spoil," and as our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Avot 1:15), "Make your Torah study fixed, and your work occasional."
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 2:15: It follows that when bad character traits are fixed in a person, he is prevented from fulfilling the Torah and its commandments; and even if he does fulfill them, it will not be for the sake of Heaven, and only with great difficulty — and of him it is said (Proverbs 11:22), "Like a golden ring in a pig's snout..." for his impurity is still clothed within him, within the kelipot. And as our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Yoma 72b): if he merits it, his Torah becomes for him an elixir of life; if he does not merit it, it becomes for him a deadly poison. But when he overcomes his inclination and fights against it, and removes his bad character traits from himself through effort, and fulfills the Torah and the commandments, he is called a complete tzaddik (righteous man), one who fears Heaven, a mighty man who subdues his inclination. And as he continues to conduct himself and grows more accustomed to this, until all his bad character traits are entirely removed from him and his soul no longer desires them at all, and he acquires the good character traits as an inborn nature, and no longer needs to fight with the evil inclination, because his body and his foundational soul are cleansed of all the dross of matter — as it is said to Moses (Exodus 3:5), "Remove your shoes from your feet," as mentioned in the Sefer HaTikkunim (Tikkun 31 and Tikkun 48) — then the four letters of Havayah will clothe themselves within him, and he will become a holy throne for His Chariot, blessed be He; and this man is called one who loves the Omnipresent out of love, and is called a complete chasid, perfect in every kind of perfection.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 3:1-3: A clear explanation of the term tzaddik or chasid, and how a person fulfills these two categories in actual practice:

Behold, the man whose spirit moves him to purify and sanctify himself, to accept upon himself the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven in its truth, should prepare himself with all his strength and hasten to fulfill all 613 commandments; for by their fulfillment, the 613 limbs and sinews of his intellective soul are completed, as mentioned (in the First Gate). For if he lacks even one commandment from the 248 positive commandments, he still lacks one limb of his soul, and of him it is said (Ecclesiastes 1:15), "and what is lacking cannot be counted" — and this is more severe than the general rule that "any man who has a blemish shall not draw near." But one who has fulfilled them all yet transgressed even one of the 365 negative commandments is called a person with an actual blemish, for the conduit and sinew that draws the flow to the limbs has become twisted; and of him it is said (ibid.), "that which is twisted cannot be made straight" — meaning, after his passing from the world, for there is no more opportunity for the performance of the deeds of the missing commandments, called "ma'aseh" (deed), nor for repentance to rectify the transgressions, except in this world — as Scripture says (Ecclesiastes 9:10), "for there is no deed, nor reckoning, nor knowledge..." meaning: there is no "deed" regarding the positive commandments, no "reckoning" regarding the negative commandments, and no "knowledge" of the Torah itself, "in the grave (Sheol) where you are going." It follows that as long as one has not fulfilled all 613 commandments, he is called a tzaddik who is not complete; for it was not for nothing that Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, prayed prayers numbering as "Va'etchanan" [515, by gematria] to enter the Land, but rather to complete his soul through the fulfillment of all 613 commandments. And when he fulfills them all, yet the good character traits have not yet been fully acquired within him except through his struggle with the evil inclination, he is called a complete tzaddik who subdues his inclination. But when all the good traits become implanted in him as a complete second nature, so that he fulfills the 613 commandments with joy, out of love, without any stirring of the evil inclination at all — because his material substance has been entirely refined — as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 109:22), "and my heart is wounded within me," and he also said (ibid. 131:1), "O Lord, my heart is not haughty... my soul is like a weaned child with its mother" — it appears as if all these traits had been implanted in him from the moment he left his mother's womb — this is called a complete chasid. For thus was King David, peace be upon him, a man in whom the good traits were implanted by nature, and through the fulfillment of the commandments he called himself a chasid, as he said (ibid. 86:2), "Guard my soul, for I am a chasid (pious one)."
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 3:4: And likewise our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Bava Kamma 30a), "Whoever wishes to be a chasid should fulfill the teachings of Pirkei Avot" — in which the acquisition of good character traits is mentioned, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Avot 2:1), "Rabbi says, which is the right path..." and Akavya ben Mahalalel says (ibid. 3:1), "Reflect upon three things..." and likewise (ibid. 4:4) Rabbi Levitas of Yavneh says, "Be exceedingly, exceedingly lowly of spirit..." And this is what Akavya intended when he said "and you will not come to sin" — meaning, you will not come under the power of the evil inclination that causes you to sin, for the evil inclination itself will be nullified within you; for if the evil inclination still existed and merely restrained itself by strength from transgressing, he should have said, "and you do not commit a transgression."
